newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 20.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - Jan 20.

text.p: The government will investigate stopping accident compensation to drunken drivers who cause serious injury. The Accident Compensation Corporation now has to take claimants to court if it wants to stop them getting payouts, and the change would be a significant move away from the present no-fault system. A spokeswoman for ACC and Transport Minister Jenny Shipley said the government had agreed to investigate giving ACC the right to withhold payouts to injured drunken drivers. However, the government's coalition agreement says it will give ACC the right to withhold benefits from convicted drunken drivers who cause serious injury. Page 1.

Bill Mansfield would not accept any redundancy payout after resigning from his job as director-general of the Conservation Department, he said on Sunday. Executive manager strategic development Keith Johnston said he and Mansfield had made it quite clear there would be no such payout. Mansfield, who announced his resignation on Friday, said he would neither ask for, nor receive, any compensation for his resignation, seven months short of the end of his contract. Page 1.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger has asked the inspector-general of intelligence, Laurie Greig, to investigate the Social Welfare Department's use of the SIS to sweep offices for listening devices, according to a letter sent to Alliance spokesman Matt Robson. Robson said on Sunday he had written to Bolger asking if there had been an inquiry into Social Welfare's use of the Security Intelligence Service. He said Bolger had said there had not been one, but agreed to Robson's request that one be started. Page 2.

The mediterranean fruitfly infestation has cost the government $6.6 million and the horticulture industry "significantly more", the Agriculture Ministry says. A further $19 million will be spent over the next three years to prevent infected fruit being brought into New Zealand. In its briefing papers to the incoming governmeent, written in October, the ministry says it remains concerned at the "continuing level of risk" from passengers arriving at Auckland International Airport. Page 2.

Any plans for separate Maori prison units were a long way off, a Corrections Department spokeswoman said on Sunday. Alison Welch said the department had been negotiating with Maori educator Pita Sharples about contracting him to provide advice for such units. Reports of an entirely separate prison for Maoris, with different rules and conditions, were premature, she said. Page 3.

The soundness of banks is hard to judge because of a weakness in the new disclosure regime, according to Massey University banking studies senior lecturer David Tripe. In an analysis of the disclosure regime for the September 1996 quarter, Tripe says that banks are not required to identify their exposure to fixed and capped rate loans. Page 11.

The Wallis inquiry into Australia's financial system is meeting Reserve Bank governor Don Brash and bank officials in Wellington tomorrow. All five members of the inquiry, headed by prominent Australian businessman Stan Wallis, arrive in New Zealand today for talks. The inquiry will also meet the Securities Commission and Australian-owned financial institutions operating here. Page 11.
